title: AGI May Already Be Here This Year; What's Left Is Turning It Into Money
dek: Chamath's judgment is that AGI has essentially existed since the start of this year, and the only difference is the pace at which closed labs choose to release it — the gap will be closed within three to four months. The real bottleneck isn't benchmarks, it's how companies and ordinary people organise it into something with ROI.
why: The first half is an argument about AI valuations, organisational form and EA conflicts of interest; the last forty minutes suddenly turn to the equity structure of a Venezuela oil deal.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching AI valuations and the bubble, the open-versus-closed fight, and US geopolitical energy deals.
skip: If you only care about AI, the Venezuela oil segment after 01:20 can be skipped.

points.h: AGI may already have arrived at the start of the year
points.body: Chamath's judgment is blunt: AGI has essentially existed since the start of this year, and the only difference is the pace at which closed frontier labs are agonising over releasing it. He expects these capabilities to be matched or nearly matched by a handful of closed alternatives and open-source alternatives within the next three to four months. So for most people the thing to watch isn't the benchmark chart but two things: top-tier intelligence is being widely accessed, and the cost of each incremental unit of intelligence keeps being pushed down. What's left is the ‘messy middle’ — how companies and people organise it into something with ROI. His advice is keep calm and carry on.

points.h: Use one bot to manage all your bots
points.body: He built a bot called improve my bots bot, had it walk through all his bots, fill in skills and instructions, and improve them once a day. The bot volunteered that merging two or three of them into a single instruction set would be better, then executed all the changes itself, and he estimates his bots got 30% to 40% better on average. Another cheap hack is to just ask your chief bot ‘what else should I be using you for’, and it will suggest the next step. The move here is turning tuning into a continuously running daily task rather than a one-off manual job.

points.h: This time it's real money, but 50x is still dangerous
points.body: Freeberg points out the key difference from the internet bubble: back then the whole boom was built on numbers that weren't dollars, like website hits and pageviews; what we see now is revenue, profit, and revenue and profit growth. Chamath adds that the Anthropic story, data centres, infrastructure, networking gear — all of it is real dollars moving, not speculative utilization. But he also issues a pricing warning: companies being priced at 50 to 100 times top-line revenue is unsustainable — giving a one-on-one legendary founder like Elon or Travis 30 times revenue makes sense, but unproven founders getting 50x, 100x is dangerous, because entry price matters. He also says that if this batch of companies loses 95% of its market cap within six months, the long tail below will simply go under, with people leaving the office carrying Aeron chairs.

points.h: Founders should take money, but Series A cash-out is a negative signal
points.body: Chamath gives founders two pieces of advice: you have the right to sell 10% to 20% of your stake now, especially if this is your first company and you haven't yet built up a principal; and if you plan to delay a raise by six months so the valuation can double or triple, that's a huge mistake — if you can get $100 million, $250 million, $1 billion into the cap table at a solid valuation or 10 to 40 times revenue, take it. Companies holding hundreds of millions to billions in cash have optionality, and can survive a real retreat. Freeberg explicitly objects to applying this to early-stage companies: a Series A founder wanting to cash out is, in his view, a huge negative signal; selling stock in a company that has no revenue yet feels like a lack of confidence in your own company.

points.h: Two IPOs will release half a trillion in charitable money
points.body: Once Anthropic and OpenAI go public, the charitable donations or DAF money the two companies generate will together exceed half a trillion dollars, possibly more. That money will be allocated through one specific lens — effective altruism — and will inevitably shape outcomes, just as the capital of Soros, the Koch family and Sheldon Adelson each shaped outcomes. Chamath says he doesn't judge whether EA is right or wrong; the only problem is that conflicts of interest aren't adequately disclosed: A writes articles, A shares an office with B, B's wife works under someone in charge at a frontier lab, B also holds $5 million of Anthropic, C works at Anthropic, everyone is roommates and co-invests. These relationships aren't a problem in themselves — the PayPal Mafia had its own version back then — the difference is not disclosing.

points.h: The main line of AI politics has shifted to open versus closed
points.body: For the past few years the main line of AI political debate was accelerationists versus doomers, and it was bipartisan: there were progressives like Bernie Sanders who are anti-progress and anti-innovation, and conservatives like Steve Bannon who fear new technology. Now the debate is shifting to open versus closed. Sachs's judgment is that the technology won't be stopped, because consumers are adopting it — data centres get built because consumers and enterprises demand it, and adoption is pulling the whole thing forward. In the same segment Chamath rates the Hugging Face deal very highly: building, inside the largest and best-capitalised companies, a fortress against the madness of the closed-source oligopoly, letting the best ideas win in the market; he says he doesn't want to be rugpulled into an oligopoly or duopoly market structure by manufactured panic.

points.h: Two hundred accounts are enough to fake a consensus
points.body: Axios reported that roughly 200 accounts suspected of coming from Chinese platforms tried to influence Americans against AI data centres. Jason draws a more general mechanism from this: a small number of social media accounts, constantly bombarding and swarming the replies, can shape opinion and make people wrongly believe a consensus exists. He distinguishes this clearly from real public opinion — the real consensus isn't that people dislike data centres, it's that a bunch of bots are telling influential people that people dislike data centres.

points.h: The Pentagon takes 35% equity in the oil contract
points.body: North American Blue Energy Partners got a 100-year concession on 17 oil fields, involving 65 billion barrels of reserves that were previously controlled by Russian, Chinese and Maduro entities. The US government controls 55% of the deal, of which the Pentagon takes 35% equity, and the State Department gets the right to buy 20% of output at cost, with the agreement signed by Rubio and Hegseth with Venezuela's interim president. Faced with ‘should you seize another country's oil fields’, Sacks's answer is that this doesn't count as nation-building: no army, no government, no teaching American-style democracy, just a commercial transaction. His technical argument is that US shale produces light sweet crude, diesel and other distillates come from heavy crude, and Gulf Coast refineries were originally designed for heavy oil — converting them to handle light oil is very expensive.
